directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; true old Redstreak stock is rare today and is distinct from the unrelated modern Somerset Redstreak cider apple still grown in the West Country. Promoted across Herefordshire orchards by Lord Scudamore of Holme Lacy in the seventeenth century, Redstreak became the most celebrated English cider apple of its era, praised by writers including John Evelyn and immortalized in John Philips's 1708 poem 'Cyder' as the apple behind England's finest regional cider. The small, red-streaked fruit is far too astringent and acidic for fresh eating, but it was prized for producing a notably strong, richly flavored cider that for generations set the standard against which other English ciders were measured. Old true-to-name Redstreak stock has become exceedingly rare in modern cultivation, preserved mainly in historic orchard collections and by cider historians rather than offered through ordinary commercial nurseries.

common_name: Oullins Golden Gage Plum (French Golden Gage, Parent of Opal)

planting.note: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site; Oullins Golden Gage is self-fertile and does not require a second variety for pollination, though a compatible European plum improves yield.

directions: Set out dormant bare-root trees in early spring before bud break in fertile, well-drained soil in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site; Oullins Golden Gage is self-fertile and does not require a second variety for pollination, though a compatible European plum improves yield. Raised in Oullins, near Lyon in France, in the mid-nineteenth century, this golden-yellow gage-type plum combines the rich, sweet flavor gage connoisseurs prize with a far more vigorous, reliably heavy-cropping tree than many of the more temperamental English dessert gages. The round to oval fruit has thin, translucent yellow skin, sometimes lightly spotted with red where exposed to full sun, over juicy, sweet flesh good for fresh eating, cooking, and bottling alike, ripening in mid-to-late summer ahead of many main-season European plums. It has also served as parent stock in later plum breeding, including the Swedish-bred early dessert plum Opal; prune only in summer to reduce the risk of silver leaf disease, and thin crowded fruit in a heavy-cropping year to improve size.
